original_value: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent difficulties including repetitive patterns of behavior known as stereotypical motor movements (SMM). So far, several techniques have been implemented to track and identify SMMs. In this context, we propose a deep learning approach for SMM recognition, namely, convolutional neural networks (CNN) in time and frequency-domains. To solve the intrasubject SMM variability, we propose a robust CNN model for SMM detection within subjects, whose parameters are set according to a proper analysis of SMM signals, thereby outperforming state-of-the-art SMM classification works. And, to solve the intersubject variability, we propose a global, fast, and light-weight framework for SMM detection across subjects which combines a knowledge transfer technique with an SVM classifier, therefore resolving the “real-life” medical issue associated with the lack of supervised SMMs per testing subject in particular. We further show that applying transfer learning across domains instead of transfer learning within the same domain also generalizes to the SMM target domain, thus alleviating the problem of the lack of supervised SMMs in general.

result.paraphrase: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by persistent difficulties, including repetitive behavior patterns called stereotypical motor movements (SMM). Several methods have been used so far to track and identify SMMs. In this context, we present a deep learning method for SMM recognition based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) in both the time and frequency domains. To address intrasubject SMM variability, we introduce a robust CNN model for detecting SMMs within subjects, with parameters chosen through an appropriate analysis of SMM signals, outperforming state-of-the-art SMM classification methods. To handle intersubject variability, we propose a global, fast, and lightweight framework for cross-subject SMM detection that combines a knowledge transfer technique with an SVM classifier, thereby addressing the “real-life” medical challenge caused by the lack of supervised SMMs for each testing subject. We also demonstrate that transfer learning across domains, rather than within the same domain, generalizes to the SMM target domain and helps alleviate the broader problem of limited supervised SMMs.
